title.text: This is FunWiki. Wikipedia, as a map.

problem.text: Wikipedia has nearly seven million English articles, and each one is a wall of text with hundreds of blue links.
You can read it top to bottom, or you can get lost. We wanted to see how an idea connects before diving in.

home.text: FunWiki opens on a front page built from today's Wikipedia: the picture of the day, the most-read articles, and a search box.
Type any topic and its map appears straight away: the links from its opening paragraph, in the order the article mentions them.

map.text: Search for Black hole, and the article opens as a living map.
The red node is the article. Every other node is a topic its opening paragraph links to.
Hover over one, and its connections light up.
Drag it, and the map moves with you, then settles.
Double-click Gravity, and a new branch grows out of it, with Gravity's own links.
Click any topic to read about it on the right, then map it to make it the new centre.

summary.text: Your guide is Meta's Muse Spark.
Ask Muse for a simple summary, and it rewrites the article so a ten-year-old could follow it.
Every answer is grounded in Wikipedia's own text.
Switch to five bullets for the key facts instead.

path.text: Not sure where to start? Plan a path.
Muse picks topics from the map and puts them in order, easiest first, then draws the path on the map as a red trail.
Click a step to jump to it.

quiz.text: Muse writes questions from the article, and the options are shuffled, so position gives nothing away.
You see right and wrong straight away.

how.text: Under the hood: a React map that runs its own physics,
serverless functions on Vercel that cache Wikipedia's free APIs,
and one model, Muse Spark, for every AI feature.
If Muse is unavailable, FunWiki falls back to Wikipedia's own text, so the map always works.

close.text: Try it at funwiki dot vercel dot app.
